judge_assessment.explanation: Both hard failures are exact. On the equation problems the worksheet demands three things and verification records one. Problem 3 asks '(a) State the domain: for what values of x is the left side defined?' before solving, and id 3 is a single `solve` returning [9]. Problem 7 says 'You should get two candidates' then 'Test both candidates in the ORIGINAL equation', and id 7 records only the survivor [3]; the same holds for problem 10 ([4], with -1 rejected) and problem 12(a) ([1], with -3 rejected). The rejected candidates and the domain conditions are printed answers with nothing behind them — and the author plainly knew the values, because they are written into the entries' `note` fields ('Domain x >= -7', 'Squaring yields x = 3 and x = -1'). verify.py's own comment at :749 confirms notes are 'reporting tags, never gating', so those strings are documentation the machine never reads. The second failure is exact too: problems 1, 7, 8, 9 and 12 each end in an explicit explanation demand and gate_chain_manual_flags is false. I recomputed all twelve results in SymPy, including both branches of the challenge — sqrt(2x+7)=x+2 giving 1 with -3 extraneous, and sqrt(2x+7)=x+1 giving +-sqrt(6) with -sqrt(6) extraneous — and every value matches the key. REJECT is correct.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 10's rejected candidate is chosen with real care. x = -1 sits INSIDE the radical's domain (x >= -5) and still fails, because it makes the right-hand side x-1 negative. That separates the two distinct conditions a radical equation imposes, and stops 'in the domain' being learned as a synonym for 'valid'.

The challenge in problem 12 is a genuine controlled experiment: sqrt(2x+7)=x+2 and sqrt(2x+7)=x+1 differ by one constant, and that single change turns a rational solution into +-sqrt(6) with one root extraneous. Same radicand, same method, different outcome — which is a far better argument for checking than any instruction to check.

The four task types are named in the directions ('rewrite, combine, solve, or approximate') and the student is told the kinds alternate, so method choice is an explicit demand rather than an accident of ordering.

The approximation problems insist on the exact form first — problem 4 'Show the simplified exact form as well as the decimal', problem 8 'Simplify and combine ... first. Then say why sqrt(2)+sqrt(8) is NOT sqrt(10)' — which is the right defence against calculator-first habits.

The declared traps are the real errors, machine-checked as distinguishable: 6.32 from halving the radicand of sqrt(20), 3.16 from adding radicands to get sqrt(10), and -4 from making 16^(-1/2) negative instead of reciprocal.

root_causes.description: A radical equation's answer is a solution set PLUS the argument that produced it, and the contract can only express the set. Squaring is not an equivalence, so the candidates and the rejection are not working — they are the answer. Verifying only survivors verifies the one part of the process that squaring cannot corrupt.
evidence: SKILL.md:189 — 'verification hard-fails unless every problem id 1..N has at least one check (use `manual` for the unverifiable ones), so a partially-verified answer key can never slip through'. The trailing promise does not follow from the rule: the rule counts PROBLEMS, the promise is about ANSWERS.
scripts/verify.py:2020 — the coverage gate is `missing = [i for i in range(1, problem_count + 1) if i not in ids]`, i.e. membership of the id set, never a count of printed response slots

tests/check_layout.py:47-49 and ANSWER_RE at :99 — the layout gate requires that each item CONTAIN one answer-location macro; it never compares that count against the number of verify entries carrying the id
verify.json ids 3, 7, 10 and 12 are `solve` entries recording survivors only ([9], [3], [4], [1])
worksheet.tex problem 7(a) 'You should get two candidates'; 7(b) 'Test both candidates in the ORIGINAL equation'
scripts/verify.py:749 — 'standard', 'difficulty' and 'bloom' are 'reporting tags, never gating'; `note` sits in the same _UNIVERSAL_FIELDS set, so 'Domain x >= -7' in id 3's note is never read

root_causes.description: Five of twelve problems end in an explicit explanation demand and none is declared, which is the SKILL.md:249-vs-:257 tension again. The sheet's format field is machine_first, and the author appears to have read that as a reason to avoid manual entries altogether rather than as a statement about the majority of items.
evidence: SKILL.md:249 — 'Reserve `manual` for genuinely open reasoning (proofs, "explain why", construction)'. 'Reserve' is rationing language and is what an author follows when deciding a single sentence is not worth a manual entry.

SKILL.md:257 — 'Use `manual` for: graph sketches, sign charts, word problem setups, two-column proofs, constructions, Riemann sum tables, series convergence arguments, and any explanation/reasoning answer.' This clause is broad and correct, and it is the one that is being ignored.
Neither line is enforced: no gate reads the worksheet prose for an imperative like 'explain', 'say in one sentence', 'name the error' or 'state whether'

worksheet.tex problem 1 'Say in one sentence what the exponent 1/2 instructs you to do'; 7(b) 'explain in one sentence why the other one fails'; 8 'say why sqrt(2)+sqrt(8) is not sqrt(10)'; 9 'state whether the result is positive or negative before you compute it'; 12(c) 'explain why squaring is what makes the extraneous-root check necessary'
final_response.md: 'All 12 worksheet problems (13 verify entries) are machine-verified — 0 manual'

improvements.title: Domain restrictions and extraneous-root rejections are stated in prose and verified nowhere
improvements.proposed_change: Both halves are expressible with types verify.py ALREADY has, so this needs no schema growth. (a) Domains: use `inequality`, whose signature is {expr, relation, expected} with an interval spec — problem 3's domain becomes {"id": 3, "type": "inequality", "expr": "x + 7", "relation": ">=", "expected": [-7, "oo", "closed"]}, and problem 10's sign condition becomes the same shape on x - 1. (b) Rejections: use `eval` on the ORIGINAL equation at the rejected candidate, so the failure is demonstrated rather than asserted — for problem 7, evaluating sqrt(2*x+3) at x = -1 gives 1 while x gives -1, and the mismatch IS the rejection. Then enforce it: in verify.py, when a `solve` entry's expression contains a radical (or any even root) and the squared polynomial has more real roots than the expected list, require a companion entry per discarded root, or fail naming it. That condition is exactly computable and it fires only on the sheets where extraneous roots are possible.
improvements.regression_test: Add a verify.py unit test: {"type": "solve", "expr": "sqrt(2*x+3) - x", "expected": [3]} as the sole entry for its id must fail with a message naming the discarded candidate x = -1; adding an eval of sqrt(2*x+3) at x = -1 must make it pass. Today the lone solve passes silently.
improvements.expected_impact: This is the stated focus of the task — 'combining radical equations, domains, and approximate solutions'. Four of twelve problems are radical equations and all four currently verify only the part of the answer squaring cannot damage. It also turns the author's existing `note` prose into checked data rather than commentary.
improvements.risk: Medium. Detecting 'this solve had extraneous candidates' requires squaring the equation and comparing root counts, which is cheap for these but can be expensive or non-enumerable for nested radicals. Bound it to a single radical and fall back to MANUAL rather than FAIL when the polynomial's roots are not exactly enumerable.

improvements.title: Written explanations the worksheet demands are recorded as machine-verified rather than manual
improvements.proposed_change: Declare ids 1, 7, 8, 9 and 12 manual alongside their computational entries, and gate it with the prose scan: an imperative such as 'say in one sentence', 'explain', 'state whether' or 'say why' inside a \problem segment must be matched by a manual entry under that id. Merge SKILL.md:249's 'Reserve manual for...' into :257's broader rule so an author is not choosing between two lines that point opposite ways. Note that problem 9's 'state whether the result is positive or negative' is a closed binary answer rather than open reasoning, so it is better served by the exact-answer entry than by `manual` — the scan should demand coverage, not specifically a manual type.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture problem 'Evaluate 49^(1/2). Say in one sentence what the exponent instructs you to do.' with a single eval entry; assert check_layout.py exits non-zero naming the unflagged explanation. Silent today.
improvements.expected_impact: Five of twelve problems gain honest treatment, and the sheet's delivery message stops asserting '0 manual' on a worksheet that asks for five written explanations.
improvements.risk: Medium. Keyword scans over-fire on hint clauses ('Simplify the radical first, then approximate' contains no demand). Scope to \problem segments and ship warn-only for one run.

improvements.title: final_response.md names the three deliverables but gives no filenames
improvements.proposed_change: final_response.md opens 'Three PDFs are ready: the student worksheet, a full step-by-step answer key, and a two-page skills summary' and never prints a filename, unlike eight of the ten cases in this slice, which give ws_/ak_/ss_ names. A reader cannot locate the files from the message. Have the delivery step emit the three paths build.sh already prints in its '── PDFs ──' block (gate_log.txt lines 'ws_r_curr375.pdf' etc.), so the response is generated from the build output rather than described from memory. Add a check to tests/check_artifact_health.py that final_response.md contains one occurrence of each of the three produced PDF basenames.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture final_response.md mentioning 'three PDFs' in prose with no filenames, against a build that produced ws_/ak_/ss_ PDFs; assert check_artifact_health.py exits non-zero listing the missing basenames. No such check exists today.
improvements.expected_impact: Makes the deliverable locatable. I am scoring this p2 rather than the canonical p1 because this response does name all three artifacts by role — only the filenames are missing — which is a weaker instance than a response that omits an artifact entirely.
improvements.risk: Low. The names are already printed by build.sh, so this is plumbing rather than new information.

case_summary: All twelve results are correct — I recomputed the rational exponents, both radical simplifications, all four equations with their candidate sets, and all three approximations, and every value matches the key. The design is the strongest in my slice for this topic: problem 10's rejected candidate sits inside the radical's domain and still fails, which pulls the two conditions apart, and problem 12 runs a controlled experiment where one changed constant turns a rational solution into +-sqrt(6). The rejection is right and lands on the focus itself. Four radical equations verify only their surviving solutions, so the domain conditions and the extraneous-root rejections — the reason radical equations are taught at all — are unchecked. The author knew the values and wrote them into `note` fields, which verify.py's own comments describe as never gating. Five problems end in explanation demands with zero manual entries. Both halves are fixable with types the schema already has: `inequality` for the domains, `eval` at the rejected candidate for the rejections. Separately, final_response.md names the three deliverables without filenames.
